title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 6 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 6)

content.overview: Section 6 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 permits the parties, or the arbitral tribunal with the parties' consent, to arrange administrative assistance by a suitable institution or person in order to facilitate the conduct of arbitral proceedings.
content.glance: Section 6 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 permits the parties, or the arbitral tribunal with the parties' consent, to arrange administrative assistance by a suitable institution or person in order to facilitate the conduct of arbitral proceedings.
content.study:
1. Purpose of section 6: Section 6 facilitates the conduct of arbitral proceedings through administrative assistance. It is therefore a procedural-support provision, not an independent source of adjudicatory jurisdiction.

2. Assistance arranged by the parties: The parties may arrange for administrative assistance by a suitable institution or person. The text does not make tribunal consent an additional condition where the parties themselves arrange the assistance.

3. Assistance arranged by the arbitral tribunal: An arbitral tribunal may arrange administrative assistance by a suitable institution or person only with the consent of the parties. The consent requirement must not be omitted when the arrangement originates with the tribunal.

4. Nature of the assistance: The assistance must be administrative and directed to facilitating the conduct of proceedings. Section 6 does not by itself transfer the tribunal's adjudicatory mandate to the assisting institution or person.

5. Relationship with other sources of authority: The actual powers and responsibilities of an institution or person providing administrative assistance may also depend on the arbitration agreement, incorporated institutional rules and other applicable provisions of the Act. Section 6 should not be used to invent powers that the parties or the Act have not conferred.

examples.title: Party-arranged assistance
examples.body: The parties agree to use a suitable arbitral institution for administrative support in conducting the proceedings. Section 6 permits that arrangement.

examples.title: Tribunal-arranged assistance with consent
examples.body: The tribunal proposes that a suitable institution provide administrative support and both parties consent. The statutory condition for tribunal-arranged assistance is satisfied.

examples.title: Tribunal arrangement without consent
examples.body: The tribunal unilaterally appoints an institution to provide administrative assistance despite the absence of party consent. Section 6 does not authorise that tribunal-initiated arrangement on its own.

examples.title: Administrative support is not adjudication
examples.body: An institution assists with scheduling and procedural administration. That assistance does not, by section 6 alone, give the institution authority to decide the dispute or replace the tribunal.

hypotheticals.question: The tribunal wants an institution to provide administrative support, but one party does not consent. Can section 6 itself authorise the arrangement?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Where the arbitral tribunal arranges the administrative assistance, section 6 expressly requires the consent of the parties.

hypotheticals.question: Both parties directly arrange for a suitable institution to provide administrative assistance. Is tribunal consent required by section 6?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 6 separately permits the parties to arrange administrative assistance. The statutory text does not add a tribunal-consent requirement to that party-arranged route.

hypotheticals.question: Can an institution providing administrative assistance decide the merits simply because it is involved under section 6?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 6 concerns administrative assistance to facilitate proceedings. Adjudicatory authority must come from the applicable arbitration framework and cannot be assumed from administrative involvement.

rows.left: Section 6 does not prescribe tribunal consent as an additional condition.
rows.right: Consent of the parties is expressly required.
Determines disputes and issues the adjudicatory outcome.

misconceptions.trap: The tribunal can arrange administrative assistance without party consent.
misconceptions.correction: Section 6 expressly requires consent of the parties when the arbitral tribunal arranges the assistance.

misconceptions.trap: Section 6 gives an assisting institution power to decide the dispute.
misconceptions.correction: The section concerns administrative assistance; adjudicatory authority must arise from the applicable arbitration framework.

misconceptions.trap: Only an arbitral institution can provide assistance.
misconceptions.correction: The statutory wording permits a suitable institution or person.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does section 6 permit?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: It permits the parties, or the arbitral tribunal with the consent of the parties, to arrange administrative assistance by a suitable institution or person to facilitate the conduct of arbitral proceedings.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The provision is facilitative and administrative.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the principal objection to tribunal-arranged assistance without consent?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 6 expressly conditions tribunal-arranged administrative assistance on the consent of the parties. The record should therefore establish consent before the tribunal's arrangement is treated as authorised under this provision.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The submission should identify the statutory initiator-and-consent structure.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should ACA section 6 be applied?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the statutory trigger, conditions, exceptions and consequence and apply them to the facts.

examTips: State the purpose: administrative assistance to facilitate proceedings.
For tribunal-arranged assistance, prove party consent.
Do not equate administrative assistance with adjudicatory power.
Check the arbitration agreement and applicable institutional rules for additional authority.
